title: Holding data back
objectives: Evaluate a model on data it was not fitted on.

screens.title: One split, one number
screens.prose: Our 200 loans are a cross-section: each row is a different borrower, and the row order means nothing. Rows like these are **exchangeable**, so a random split is fair. A real book is issued over time; for loans with issue dates, use time-ordered folds, as in level 2. We fit a linear model for spread on 150 loans and test it on the other 50.

Both improve, so the bigger the test set the better.
options.why: You read only the solid line. The dashed average rises, because a model fitted on 100 loans is worse than one fitted on 180.

options.text: The spread grows, since more test loans add more errors.

The solid line is the spread, the dashed line the average.
At 10% the sd is 0.058 and the average 0.207. At 50% they are 0.022 and 0.215.

screens.title: Three sets, three jobs
screens.prose: The 50 loans we held back are a **test set**: rows the model never saw while it was fitted. When we must also choose between models, we hold back a second slice, the **validation set**. The rest is the **training set**. Here 400 loans are split 60/20/20.
screens.question: Drag each job into the set that does it: **Fit** the coefficients, **Pick** between models, **Report** the final score.

hints.text: Which set must stay untouched until the very end?
The final score needs rows that took no part in fitting or choosing.
Fit on training rows, compare candidates on validation rows, and score once on test rows.

feedback.correct: Training fits, validation chooses, test reports once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each set has exactly one job.

byKey.fit: Fitting belongs on the training rows. Fitting on rows that later judge the model lets it mark its own homework.
byKey.pick: Choosing needs rows the fit did not see, but not the test rows: they are kept for one final score.
byKey.report: The final score must come from rows that played no part in fitting or choosing: the test set.

explain.text: You gave each set one job. Training rows fit the coefficients, validation rows compare candidates, and test rows give one final score. Touch the test rows twice and they become a second validation set.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def split_three(X, y, n_val, n_test, seed):
    order = np.random.default_rng(seed).permutation(len(y))
    test = np.sort(order[:n_test])
    val = np.sort(order[n_test:n_test + n_val])
    train = np.sort(order[n_test + n_val:])
    return train, val, test

tests.setup: X, y = make_loans(400, 8, 21); parts = split_three(X, y, 80, 80, 5)
tests.call: sorted(int(i) for a in parts for i in a) == list(range(400))

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests that compare your row numbers exactly, on 10 to 400 loans. `make_loans(n, p, seed)` is defined for you. This screen uses NumPy only; the first run loads it, which takes a few seconds.
widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

def make_loans(n, p, seed):
    """Loans: spread over base rate (percentage points). x0 leverage +0.6, x1 interest cover -0.4,
    x2 sector risk +0.3, the rest pure noise; noise sd 0.45."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, p)).round(3)
    beta = np.zeros(p)
    beta[:3] = [0.6, -0.4, 0.3][:p]
    y = (2.5 + X @ beta + rng.normal(0, 0.45, n)).round(3)
    return X, y

hints.text: Slice `order` three times.
Test is `order[:n_test]`.
Validation is `order[n_test:n_test + n_val]`, training is `order[n_test + n_val:]`; wrap each in `np.sort`.

feedback.correct: The same seed always rebuilds the same three sets.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. For 10 rows, `n_val=2`, `n_test=3`, seed 0 the answer is train `[0, 1, 5, 8, 9]`, validation `[3, 7]`, test `[2, 4, 6]`.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Replace each `...` with a slice of `order`.

explain.text: One permutation, cut into three pieces, keeps the sets disjoint and covers every row. Sorting makes the output easy to compare. The seed is the receipt: with it, a reviewer gets your exact split.

screens.title: The luckiest split
screens.prose: A colleague runs the same model with seeds 0 to 19. The lowest test MSE is 0.142, from seed 15. Their slide says “test MSE 0.142”.

state.caption: Twenty splits of the same 200 loans.

screens.question: What should the slide report?

options.text: 0.142, the best split
options.why: You kept the luckiest of 20 draws. The minimum of 20 noisy numbers sits well below their centre, so it flatters the model.

options.text: The mean of all 20 splits, 0.210, with their spread, about 0.05
0.286, the worst split, to be safe
options.why: You swapped one extreme for the other. The maximum is as unrepresentative as the minimum.

options.text: 0.142, because seed 15 is written down and anyone can reproduce it
options.why: A recorded seed makes the number repeatable, not representative. Picking the seed after seeing the scores is the problem.

hints.text: Would seed 15 still win if we drew 50 new loans?
The highlighted bar is the minimum of twenty draws.
Every split is equally valid, so report what they say together: their mean and spread.

feedback.correct: Report all twenty together, or one split fixed before looking.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which number a fresh split would most likely give.

byKey.min: You reported the best of 20 splits. That number was chosen because it was low, so it is biased low.
byKey.seed: You leaned on reproducibility. Choosing the seed after seeing the scores is still choosing.

explain.text: The twenty splits average 0.210 with an sd of about 0.05. The minimum, 0.142, is what you get by choosing after looking. Fix the seed before you see any score, or report every split.

screens.title: Edge case: five test loans
screens.prose: Now each split holds back only 5 loans. The ten seeds give test MSEs from 0.054 to 0.411, an sd of 0.11: half the size of the thing we are measuring.
screens.question: A new book has only 40 loans. What is the honest way to measure a model on it?

options.text: Let every loan take a turn in a small test set, and average all the turns
Hold back 5 loans once; the number is unbiased
options.why: Unbiased is not enough. With 5 loans the sd is about half the MSE itself, so one number tells us little.

options.text: Score the model on the loans it was fitted on
options.why: You used training error. The model has seen those loans, so its error there is too low.

options.text: Skip testing: 40 loans is too few to bother
options.why: Small data is where overfitting bites hardest, so measuring matters more, not less.

hints.text: The trouble is noise, not bias.
Each 5-loan test set is tiny, but there are eight disjoint ones in 40 loans.
If every loan is tested once and the results averaged, all 40 loans count towards the score.

feedback.correct: That is cross-validation, the subject of lesson 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a way to use every loan for testing.

explain.text: One 5-loan test set is too noisy to read. Rotating the test rows lets every loan be tested once, so the average uses all 40. Lesson 2 builds exactly that.

screens.title: Why bigger test sets are steadier
screens.prose: A test MSE is the average of $n_{\text{test}}$ squared errors $e_i^2$. An average of independent terms has sd $\text{sd}(e^2)/\sqrt{n_{\text{test}}}$. For normal errors $\text{Var}(e^2) = 2\sigma^4$, so $$\text{sd}(\widehat{\text{MSE}}) \approx \sigma^2\sqrt{\frac{2}{n_{\text{test}}}}.$$ Our loans have $\sigma^2 = 0.2025$: 50 test loans give about 0.04.
screens.question: What sd does a 200-loan test set give, with $\sigma^2 = 0.2025$?

feedback.correct: Four times the test loans, half the spread.

byKey.same: That is the 50-loan value. Put $n = 200$ under the square root.
byKey.linear: You divided by 4. The sd shrinks with the square root of $n$, so four times the loans halves it.

explain.text: $0.2025 \times \sqrt{2/200} = 0.2025 \times 0.1 = 0.0203$. The resplits we saw spread a little less, 0.035 at 50 loans, because they reuse the same 200 loans. The square root is why halving the noise costs four times the data.

screens.title: Was the test set touched?
screens.prose: A project log lists events as `(action, rows)` pairs, such as `('fit', 'train')` or `('score', 'val')`. The rule: the test rows may appear once, as `('final', 'test')`, and nowhere else. Any other use of the test rows, or a second final score, means the test set was touched.

state.caption: Touched: the test rows were scored before the final score.

screens.title: The locked years
screens.prose: A credit desk keeps the last two years of loans locked until a model is frozen. In March, an analyst scores a draft on the locked years “just to look”. It does badly, so she drops two features and scores it again.
screens.question: What are the locked years now?

options.text: A validation set: they helped choose the features, so the desk needs a new untouched test set
Still a test set, because she looked only once before changing the model
options.why: You counted looks, not uses. One look that changes the model is enough to make those years part of the choosing.

options.text: Still a test set, as long as she reports only the second score
options.why: The second model was picked after seeing the first score, so its score on the same years is no longer clean.

options.text: Training data, because the model has been fitted on them
options.why: She did not fit on them; she chose with them. Rows that guide a choice are validation rows.

hints.text: What did the first score change?
Ask whether the final model would be the same if she had never looked.
The years influenced which features survived. That is the job of a validation set.

feedback.correct: The locked years became validation data the moment they changed the model.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the locked years influenced the final model.

explain.text: Her look led to a change, so the locked years now carry information into the model. Their score is no longer an outside view. The desk must wait for new loans, or lock a fresh slice, to get one.

screens.title: Best of 20
screens.prose: A research note says “test Sharpe 1.4 (best of 20 splits)”. Suppose the signal’s test Sharpe across splits has mean 0.6 and sd 0.4. The largest of 20 normal draws sits, on average, 1.87 sds above their mean.
screens.question: What best-of-20 Sharpe would a signal with a true Sharpe of 0.6 typically show?

hints.text: Start from the mean and add some sds.
The best of 20 sits 1.87 sds up.

feedback.correct: About 1.35: the note’s 1.4 is what a 0.6 signal shows as its best of 20.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add 1.87 sds of 0.4 to the mean of 0.6.

byKey.mean: That is the typical split. The note reports the best of 20, which sits well above it.
byKey.nosd: You added 1.87 itself. Multiply by the sd, 0.4, first.

explain.text: $0.6 + 1.87 \times 0.4 = 1.35$. A headline of 1.4 is what selection alone gives a 0.6 signal. Ask for all 20 splits, or one split fixed before any score was seen.

quiz.prose: A notebook calls `train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2)` with no `random_state`.
quiz.question: Why should the seed be recorded?

options.text: So the exact split can be rebuilt, and nobody can quietly rerun until the score looks good
Because a fixed seed gives a lower test MSE
options.why: A seed makes the split repeatable; it does not make it better. Some seeds give lower scores purely by luck.

options.text: Because an unseeded split is biased
options.why: Each random split is fair. The problem is that an unrecorded one cannot be checked or repeated.

feedback.correct: The recorded seed is the receipt for the split.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about a reviewer trying to repeat your number.

explain.text: Without the seed, every rerun gives a new split and a new score. Recording it makes the result checkable and rules out silent reruns.

quiz.prose: With $\sigma^2 = 0.2025$, the test MSE has sd about $\sigma^2\sqrt{2/n_{\text{test}}}$.
quiz.question: How many test loans give an sd of 0.01?

explain.text: $\sqrt{2/n} = 0.01/0.2025 = 0.0494$, so $2/n = 0.00244$ and $n \approx 820$. Quartering the noise from 0.04 needs sixteen times the 50 loans.
